Where do you record a deed in Nebraska?

You record a Nebraska deed with the register of deeds in the county where the land sits. Nebraska has no statewide deed registry, so a deed for a house in Omaha goes to a different office than one for a farmhouse out west. Statutes such as 33-109 name both the register of deeds and the county clerk, because in some counties the clerk handles those duties.

The office varies in how it presents itself. In Douglas County, the Assessor and Register of Deeds share an office at 1819 Farnam Street, 4th Floor, Omaha, and checks are made out to the Douglas County Assessor/Register of Deeds. The county's fee page says it takes Visa, Mastercard, American Express and Discover. Smaller counties publish simpler pages: Chase County's register lists a post office box and a short fee schedule, and Nemaha County's page repeats the state fee schedule and the stamp tax.

Before you travel or mail anything, call the county office and ask about its accepted payment types, whether e-recording is offered, and whether it needs the original or will accept a copy. Those practices are local, and the statutes do not set them.

What do you need to bring when you record a Nebraska deed?

Bring the signed and acknowledged deed, a completed Real Estate Transfer Statement, and payment for the recording fee and any stamp tax. Missing the transfer statement is the single most common reason a deed is turned away, because 76-214 bars the register from recording without it.

ItemWhat to knowSource
Signed, acknowledged deedAcknowledgment in Nebraska is taken by a judge or court clerk, a U.S. magistrate or a notary, inside that officer's jurisdiction76-217
Form 521Signed by the grantee or an authorized agent, items 1 through 27 completed; the form carries a 07/2026 revision date on the Department of Revenue site76-214, Form 521
Recording fee$10 first page, $6 each added page33-109
Documentary stamp tax$3.32 per $1,000 of value as of July 18, 2026, unless an exemption applies76-901, Dept. of Revenue
Page layout3 by 8.5 inch blank space at top of page one; 8.5 by 11 to 8.5 by 14 inch paper23-1503.01

How should the document itself be prepared?

The page has to be built so the register can stamp and copy it, and 23-1503.01 spells out the details.

  • Leave the top three inches of the first page blank across its full width. If you do not, the register may add a page or use the back of one and charge the page fee.
  • Use black print on white paper of at least twenty-pound weight, with no watermarks. Electronic filings should be black on white.
  • Keep the type legible. A font of at least eight points is presumed to be.
  • Sign in black or dark blue ink. A digital or electronic signature is allowed.
  • Print or stamp each party's name under the signature, and keep stamps from covering any text.
  • Do not tape or attach anything over printed information on the instrument.

The statute carves out several categories from these rules, including instruments signed before August 27, 2011, documents executed outside the United States, certified government copies, and instruments formatted for court requirements. If your deed falls in one of those groups, confirm with the register of deeds which rules still apply.

What happens to the paperwork after the deed is recorded?

The register of deeds records the deed, marks the book and page on Form 521, and passes the form to the county assessor. The assessor processes it under instructions from the state's Property Tax Administrator and sends it on to the Tax Commissioner. That chain is described in 76-214, and the Form 521 instructions repeat it: the register completes items 28 through 30 when the deed is recorded, then forwards the original to the assessor and keeps a copy.

The same statute lets anyone view these statements at the Tax Commissioner's, assessor's or register's office, as long as the record has not been disposed of under the retention schedule. That is why the price and deed type you write on the form can later show up in an appraiser's or neighbor's research.

The form also includes a question about whether an affidavit under 76-2,141 is needed, which applies to property inside a county or area with an active air force ballistic missile field. Read the form instructions for that line if your county might be affected.

Does the recording date matter?

Yes. Under 76-237, a deed is recorded in the order delivered and counts as recorded from the time it is delivered to the register of deeds. Section 76-238 adds the consequence: a recorded instrument is effective against creditors and later good-faith buyers from delivery, and an unrecorded instrument is void as to a later buyer without notice who records first. The unrecorded deed remains valid between the people who signed it.

That is a practical point for sellers. If a sale closes and the buyer's deed sits unrecorded for weeks, there is a window in which a creditor's claim against the seller could be recorded first. Having the deed filed promptly after closing shortens that window.

One special deadline applies to transfer on death deeds, which must be recorded within thirty days of signing and before the owner's death. That rule is in 76-3410 and is covered in our guide to those deeds.

What other costs and special filings come up?

Beyond the standard fee, Nebraska counties charge for copies, and a few filings follow their own rules.

  • Certified copies. $1.50 per page under 33-109. Chase County's page adds that certification is charged in addition to the ordinary photocopy fee.
  • Non-certified copies. Douglas County's request page lists a $5.00 per-document charge for requests of more than ten.
  • No-fee documents. County pages say federal and state tax liens are recorded without a fee, and only when they come from the Nebraska Secretary of State.
  • Death certificates. When title passes by transfer on death deed, joint tenancy or the end of a life estate, 76-2,126 requires a death certificate to be filed with the register of deeds. For a transfer on death deed, a cover sheet naming the recorded document, grantor, surviving grantee and legal description is attached.
  • Fee earmark. $2.50 of each first-page fee and 50 cents of each added page go to records preservation and technology, according to the statute.

Fee schedules change by statute, so verify against the county office before you write a check.

Recording a deed when you sell a Nebraska home

In many sales a title or escrow company prepares the transfer statement and files the deed, though the statutes do not require one. A seller handling a family transfer or private sale carries those steps personally.

If you are selling a house that has an old unrecorded deed behind it, record it first. Buyers and lenders look to the register's index, and a gap in the chain slows everything down. We buy Nebraska houses as-is and can walk through your recorded documents with you before any offer.

More questions about Nebraska Recording a Deed

Where do I record a deed in Nebraska?

File it with the register of deeds, or the county clerk where the two offices are combined, in the county where the property is located. Douglas County, for example, takes recordings at the Assessor/Register of Deeds office at 1819 Farnam Street in Omaha.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Nebraska?

The statutory recording fee is $10 for the first page and $6 for each additional page under 33-109. A documentary stamp tax of $3.32 per $1,000 of value also applies as of July 18, 2026 unless the deed is exempt under 76-902.

Can the register of deeds refuse to record my deed?

Yes, in at least one situation the statute is explicit. Under 76-214 the register shall not record a deed if the grantee has not furnished the completed transfer statement. A deed that lacks the required blank space may also be accepted only with an added page and fee under 23-1503.01.

Is a deed valid if I do not record it?

It is valid between the parties, but under 76-238 it is void against later good-faith purchasers and creditors who record first without notice. Recording protects the new owner.

Can I get a certified copy of my recorded deed?

Yes. The statutory certified copy charge is $1.50 per page under 33-109, and the county may add its own photocopy fee. Ask the register of deeds for the book and page or search by owner name.
